Sciatica: Why Does Pain Travel from Your Lower Back to Your Leg?

Dr. Surabhi Vaidya · BAMS, MD (Ayurveda) Charak Health Solutions · Raymond TenX Habitat, Thane West
📅 November 2026 ⏱ 6 min read 🏷 Nerve & Spine

Have you experienced pain that begins around your lower back or buttock and travels down one leg?

Sometimes the pain feels sharp or burning. At other times, it may be accompanied by tingling, numbness or an electric-shock-like sensation.

You may find sitting, walking or changing positions uncomfortable.

These symptoms can occur with a condition commonly known as sciatica.

But not every pain in the back or leg is sciatica. Understanding the difference can help you decide when to seek medical attention.

What is sciatica?

Sciatica refers to symptoms caused by irritation or compression of nerve roots that contribute to the sciatic nerve.

The sciatic nerve pathway extends from the lower back through the buttock and down the leg.

When these nerves become irritated, pain and other symptoms may be felt away from the lower back.

Sciatica commonly affects one side, although symptoms can sometimes involve both legs.

What are the common symptoms of sciatica?

Sciatica may produce:

  • Pain travelling from the buttock down the leg: Often reaching below the knee into the calf or foot
  • Burning or shooting pain: May feel like sudden electric jolts during movement
  • Tingling or pins-and-needles sensations: Often felt in the toes or foot
  • Numbness in parts of the leg or foot: Reduced sensation to touch
  • Muscle weakness: Heaviness or difficulty lifting the front of the foot
  • Symptoms aggravated by certain movements: Coughing, sneezing, or sitting for long periods may worsen discomfort

Some people experience significant leg pain with relatively little discomfort in the lower back.

The location of symptoms can provide useful information, but a clinical examination may be required to understand their cause.

What causes sciatica?

Several spinal conditions may irritate or compress the relevant nerve roots:

Herniated or bulging disc

A spinal disc may protrude and irritate a nearby nerve root. However, a disc bulge visible on imaging does not always cause symptoms.

Spinal stenosis

Narrowing of spaces around the spinal nerves may contribute to nerve irritation or compression.

Age-related spinal changes

Changes in discs and facet joints over time can sometimes affect surrounding nerve structures.

The precise cause cannot always be determined from symptoms alone.

Is sciatica the same as ordinary lower back pain?

No.

Ordinary lower back pain may remain limited to the back, while sciatica typically involves nerve-related symptoms travelling into a leg.

For example, pain that extends from the buttock towards the calf or foot, especially with tingling or numbness, may suggest nerve involvement.

A clinician can help distinguish sciatica from muscular discomfort, hip-related pain and other possible conditions.

Does sciatica always need surgery?

No.

Many episodes of sciatica improve over several weeks or months, although recovery varies and some people experience longer-lasting or recurring symptoms.

Management may include:

  • Appropriate movement: Staying active within comfortable limits is often encouraged.
  • Suitable exercises: Exercises may be recommended according to the person's symptoms and examination findings.
  • Medical evaluation: A clinician may recommend appropriate treatment or investigations based on the severity and duration of symptoms.
  • Specialist care: Some people require specialist assessment, particularly when neurological deficits develop or significant pain persists.

Surgery is considered in selected cases rather than automatically recommended for everyone with sciatica.

When is sciatica a medical emergency?

🚨 Urgent Medical Emergency: Immediate Hospital Care

Certain symptoms require immediate emergency hospital assessment. Seek emergency care without delay if you experience:

  • New difficulty passing urine or losing control of your bladder
  • New loss of bowel control (fecal incontinence)
  • Numbness or loss of feeling around the groin, genitals, anus, or buttocks (saddle anesthesia)
  • Severe or rapidly worsening weakness in both legs (e.g. stumbling or inability to lift the feet)
  • Significant new numbness or weakness affecting both legs simultaneously
These red-flag signs may indicate Cauda Equina Syndrome (severe spinal nerve root compression). Do not delay emergency hospital care while waiting for a routine clinic appointment.
